stimulus.text: After 1676, Virginia's planters stopped trusting a workforce that could unite across race. White servants were politically fractious, and fewer English workers were willing to endure southern farm labor when better work could be found in the northern colonies. At the same time, the Dutch monopoly on the slave trade ended in 1682, and the price of enslaved Africans fell. A workforce held for life, whose children were born into bondage, gave planters something servants never could: workers who could never claim the liberties of Englishmen and never walk away free.

books.section: Bacon's Rebellion and the Development of Slavery in Virginia

stem: How did the end of the Dutch monopoly on the slave trade in 1682 most directly affect Chesapeake planters?

options.text: It raised the price of enslaved Africans beyond what most planters could pay.
options.misconception: The end of the monopoly lowered prices; it did not raise them.

options.text: It ended the slave trade to the English colonies entirely.
options.misconception: The trade continued and expanded; only the Dutch monopoly ended.

options.text: It forced planters to return to indentured servants for their labor.
options.misconception: Cheaper enslaved labor pulled planters further from servants, not back to them.

options.text: It lowered the price of enslaved Africans, making lifetime labor cheaper to buy.

rationales.general:
1. Name the monopoly. For years the Dutch controlled the slave trade to the English colonies.
2. Ask what a monopoly does to price. It keeps prices high, because only one seller sets the terms.
3. Read what happened in 1682. The monopoly ended, more sellers entered, and the price of enslaved Africans fell.
4. Connect the price to the planters. Cheaper lifetime labor made enslaved Africans the better buy.
Remember: when a monopoly breaks, follow the price — the buyers change their habits fast.
rationales.D: For years the Dutch held a monopoly on the slave trade to the English colonies, and a monopoly keeps prices high. When that monopoly ended in 1682, more sellers entered the trade and the price of enslaved Africans fell. Cheaper lifetime labor made enslaved Africans the better buy for Chesapeake planters, just as English servants were getting scarcer and more fractious. The other options reverse the facts: prices fell, the trade continued, and planters moved further from servants, not back to them.
rationales.A: The end of the monopoly lowered prices; it did not raise them.
rationales.B: The trade continued and expanded; only the Dutch monopoly ended.
rationales.C: Cheaper enslaved labor pulled planters further from servants, not back to them.
